prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part, B012, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After the full exchange I hold it for reasons that do not depend on how many members now name it, and the chair is right that unanimity in round 1 is convergence and not evidence. The scientific core is a mechanism that can be stated in one sentence and checked: at the magic wavelength the lattice light shift on the clock transition cancels, so a very large number of neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated in parallel on an ultranarrow line. That removes the old trade-off between confinement and accuracy, and the parallel averaging is why stability and accuracy improve together. The performance near 1e-18 has been reached and reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in several laboratories, and it already feeds tests of fundamental constants, searches for new physics and relativistic geodesy. It is both an invention and a measurement discovery in the statutory sense. On credit, the two names remain the most defensible of any shortlisted configuration: it fits under the three-person limit without forcing the choice among founders of large collaborations that Danielsson, Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce all describe as a leadership judgment and not scientific authorship. The citation should name the neutral-atom lattice scheme, so that it neither claims ion clocks nor settles priority among other lattice-clock groups.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still novelty margin: the 2005 prize (frequency combs and precision laser spectroscopy) and the 2012 prize (control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks) sit adjacent, and a committee could read lattice clocks as an outstanding refinement of one precision-timekeeping story. My answer is that neither earlier prize contains the magic-wavelength lattice or the many-atom regime, but I accept this is a judgment and cannot be shown to be correct from the record. Second, the two-name credit is a simplification. NIST, PTB, SYRTE, Japanese groups beyond Katori and the ion-clock line contributed to maturing the technology, and the relative roles of Katori's proposal, early other-group realizations and Ye's accuracy work rest on my general knowledge and not on anything in the supplied files; the chair's first question asks for exactly the verification I cannot supply. Third, a precision-metrology result may be weighed against a discovery about nature or a new class of quantum matter. I do not find that objection decisive, but I recognize it carries weight with some colleagues.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B039 to B012 but still calls the Higgs observation the most consequential experimental result on the shortlist and keeps it as his principal alternative, to be revisited if the committee can agree a defensible choice of names.
responses.response: I accept that B039 is the larger discovery in the sense of consequence, and I do not want my preference for B012 to be read as a lower assessment of the Higgs observation. My position remains that the statutes tie the prize to named persons, and you, Eriksson, Kroll and Pearce all say that a three-name selection from ATLAS and CMS rests on leadership and not identified scientific authorship, with Della Negra and Virdee equally plausible. That is not a technicality, because a prize whose credit will be disputed damages the discovery it honours. You ask in effect what would have to be true to make B039 competitive: a principled, documented rule for the three names that survives the Della Negra versus Virdee and Jenni versus Gianotti questions. Nothing in round 1 supplied that rule, so I keep B039 off my alternatives, but I would reconsider it if one were produced.

responses.point: Olsson says the lattice-clock case persuades her through breadth of support across different fields, but she shares the worry that the novelty margin over combs and ion clocks and the still-prospective impacts (redefinition of the second, geodesy) are the weak points, and she would judge the prize on demonstrated results.
responses.response: I agree that the prize should rest on demonstrated results and I would deliberately keep prospective applications out of the citation. What has been demonstrated is substantial: a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, reproduction across species and laboratories, and use in constraining constants and comparing clocks at different heights. On your novelty question I would put it this way: the comb is a counter for optical cycles and the 2012 work is about control of a single quantum object, whereas the lattice clock is a statistical instrument that gains from the number of atoms while suppressing the perturbation that confinement would otherwise cause. I also note your disclosure of stepping back on B021 and I find that the right handling. My earlier remark on its discovery content was a weighting judgment, not a criticism of the scientific quality of aberration correction.

responses.point: Johansson says that if the committee prefers a prize tied to a new quantum phenomenon rather than a metrological instrument, B057 is the better answer, and she would let B057 go forward only with a citation that is honest about the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
responses.response: This is the central question for my own fallback, since I also list B057. I agree with your qualification: the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio credits the theoretical concept of the quantum spin Hall state and the HgTe observation, but the proposal that made the HgTe experiment decisive came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and three-dimensional topological insulators add Fu and others. I do not think a citation can repair that within three names without being misleading. I therefore keep B057 as an alternative because the conceptual content is deep and the physics is mature, but I would not defend it as strongly as B012, and I do not think it should become the preferred configuration on the present record. If the committee prefers a new quantum phenomenon, I would want the attribution problem resolved first, not after the vote.

responses.point: Pearce, who chairs, moved from B029 to B012 but notes the argument that IceCube or Higgs carry more weight with the wider community than precision metrology, and says the citation should name the lattice clock specifically so as not to overreach into ion or microwave standards.
responses.response: I agree on the citation: it should name the neutral-atom lattice scheme and the magic-wavelength condition, and I have added that to my wording, so that it does not extend to ion clocks or imply that other precision optical clocks are being honoured. On the wider-community argument, I would not choose a prize on expected reception, and I think the history of precision-measurement prizes shows that a new standard of measurement can be as consequential for physics as a new particle. I do not dismiss the argument for B029 or B039 as science. For B029, your own uncertainty about allocating credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA and Baikal pioneers is the obstacle I would also see, and I think it is better to resolve that over a longer period than to force it now. On the chair's recusal question, I do not believe any of the disclosed flags changes B012: the disclosures concern B051, B021, B005 and B036 and Kroll's remote connection, and none is a documented tie to Katori or Ye.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether the lattice-clock and ion-clock lines need joint recognition, notes that part of the case rests on the pending redefinition of the second, and says she relies on memory for the early priority history.
responses.response: On joint recognition I hold my round-1 view and now add a reason from your own point about systematic shifts: the physics of lattice clocks (blackbody, higher-order light shifts, collisions between atoms in the lattice) differs from that of ion clocks, which are limited by other effects, so a joint prize would combine two different sets of problems and add names without a distinct discovery for each. On the redefinition of the second I would treat it as neither a precondition nor part of the scientific case: it is a metrological decision that will confirm the impact if it happens, and the prize should be justified without it. Your point that the early priority history should be checked against primary sources is one I support fully, and since I cannot do it from the supplied files, I list it below as an open uncertainty and not as a settled fact.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the step beyond frequency combs and single-ion control as large enough to stand as a separate prize, which is a judgment and not a fact I can establish.

The exact priority and relative roles of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, early realizations in other groups and Ye's accuracy and stability work; I rely on general knowledge, no member has verified this from the supplied record, and the chair's first question remains open for me.
Whether the formal redefinition of the second should be awaited. I regard it as having no bearing on the science, but it may affect timing and the committee's tolerance for prospective impact.

If B012 does not hold, I remain undecided between B057, where credit is incomplete without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and B036, where the mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled; neither is a configuration I would currently argue for.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: my work on turbulent particles, random matrices, stochastic dynamics and neural networks, and my documented co-authors and institutions (Gothenburg, Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg), have no stated connection to Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist. I note Johansson's disclosure of a possible tie to B051 at Chalmers; I regard that as outside B012 and my own alternatives and I have no objection to how it is being handled.
